steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the Loudness normalization section for a Wikipedia article on audio normalization, explaining how it works, why it is used, its side effects, and a short list of loudness standards by platform.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
Loudness normalization
- What it is: gain changed to reach a target average loudness
- Example (YouTube)
- Why: consistent loudness across a playlist
- Side effect: clipping, compression
### Loudness standards (list by platform)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
Loudness normalization
- normalization based on loudness: change gain so average loudness hits target level
  - average approximate (average power, e.g. RMS) or perceptual (EBU R128; ReplayGain, Sound Check, GoldWave)
- example: YouTube preferred −14 LUFS; program measured −10 LUFS -> lowered 4 dB
- combats varying loudness across songs in sequence; before it, quieter song in playlist -> listener turns volume knob up
- side effects
  - depending on dynamic range + target, peaks may exceed medium's limits -> clipping
  - software usually offers dynamic range compression to prevent it
  - then signal-to-noise ratio and relative dynamics altered

### Loudness standards
- levels vary by territory and application
- −27 to −24 LUFS: Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video
- −24 LUFS: ATSC A/85 (US TV), NPRSS, PRX radio broadcast
- −23 LUFS: EBU R 128 broadcast; Sony ASWG console/desktop games
- −19 to −16 LUFS: PRX podcasts
- −18 LUFS: Sony ASWG portable/mobile games
- −14 LUFS: Spotify, Tidal, YouTube, YouTube Shorts, TikTok

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
There is another type of normalization that is based on a measure of loudness. Here the gain is changed so that the average loudness is brought to a target level. The average can be approximate, like a simple measurement of the average power (e.g. RMS), or it can be more accurate, like a measure that takes human perception into account, e.g. the one defined by EBU R128 and offered by ReplayGain, Sound Check and GoldWave.

For example, the preferred loudness level of YouTube is −14 LUFS. So if an audio program is analyzed and it is −10 LUFS, YouTube will lower the loudness by 4 dB so it is at the preferred level.

- combats varying loudness across songs in sequence; before it, quieter song in a playlist -> listener turns volume knob up
- side effects: peaks beyond medium's limits -> clipping (depends on dynamic range, target); software offers dynamic range compression; SNR and relative dynamics altered

### Loudness standards
- vary by territory and application
- −27 to −24 LUFS: Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video
- −24 LUFS: ATSC A/85 (US TV), NPRSS, PRX radio broadcast
- −23 LUFS: EBU R 128 broadcast; Sony ASWG console/desktop games
- −19 to −16 LUFS: PRX podcasts
- −18 LUFS: Sony ASWG portable/mobile games
- −14 LUFS: Spotify, Tidal, YouTube, YouTube Shorts, TikTok

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
There is another type of normalization that is based on a measure of loudness. Here the gain is changed so that the average loudness is brought to a target level. The average can be approximate, like a simple measurement of the average power (e.g. RMS), or it can be more accurate, like a measure that takes human perception into account, e.g. the one defined by EBU R128 and offered by ReplayGain, Sound Check and GoldWave.

For example, the preferred loudness level of YouTube is −14 LUFS. So if an audio program is analyzed and it is −10 LUFS, YouTube will lower the loudness by 4 dB so it is at the preferred level.

Loudness normalization is used against varying loudness when someone listens to multiple songs in a sequence. Before there was loudness normalization, one song in a playlist could be quieter than the other songs, and then the listener would have to turn a volume knob up to adjust the playback volume.

Loudness normalization can result in peaks that are over the limits of the recording medium, which causes clipping. This depends on the dynamic range of the content and on the target level. When this happens, software that offers loudness normalization usually has the option of dynamic range compression to prevent the clipping. In this case the signal-to-noise ratio and the relative dynamics are changed.

### Loudness standards

The standardised normalized loudness levels are different depending on territory and application.

−27 LUFS to −24 LUFS: Netflix, Disney+ and Prime Video

−24 LUFS: ATSC A/85 (US TV), NPRSS and PRX radio broadcast

−23 LUFS: EBU R 128 broadcast, Sony ASWG for console and desktop games

−19 to −16 LUFS: PRX podcasts

−18 LUFS: Sony ASWG for portable and mobile games

−14 LUFS: Spotify, Tidal, YouTube, YouTube Shorts and TikTok

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Another type of normalization is based on a measure of loudness, in which the gain is changed to bring the average loudness to a target level. This average may be approximate, such as a simple measurement of average power (e.g. RMS), or more accurate, such as a measure that addresses human perception, e.g. that defined by EBU R128 and offered by ReplayGain, Sound Check and GoldWave.

For example, YouTube's preferred loudness level is −14 LUFS, so if an audio program is analyzed to be −10 LUFS, YouTube will lower the loudness by 4 dB to bring it to the preferred level.

Loudness normalization combats varying loudness when listening to multiple songs in a sequence. Before loudness normalization, one song in a playlist might be quieter than the others, so the listener would have to turn a volume knob up to adjust the playback volume.[1]

Depending on the dynamic range of the content and the target level, loudness normalization can produce peaks that exceed the recording medium's limits, causing clipping. Software offering loudness normalization typically provides dynamic range compression as an option to prevent clipping in this case. The signal-to-noise ratio and relative dynamics are then altered.

### Loudness standards

Standardised normalized loudness levels vary by territory and application.[2]

−27 LUFS to −24 LUFS: Netflix, Disney+ and Prime Video[3]

−24 LUFS: ATSC A/85 (US TV), NPRSS, and PRX radio broadcast[4,2]

−23 LUFS: EBU R 128 broadcast[2], Sony ASWG for console and desktop games[5]

−19 to −16 LUFS: PRX podcasts[6]

−18 LUFS: Sony ASWG for portable and mobile games[5]

−14 LUFS: Spotify, Tidal, YouTube, YouTube Shorts and TikTok[2]
